item.title: Improvements in Tropical Cyclone Representation in JRA-3Q over ERA5
item.description: arXiv:2611.15222v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reanalysis products are widely used for long-term tropical cyclone (TC) studies, yet the fidelity of their TC representation is not fully established. We evaluate TC representation in the recently released JRA-3Q reanalysis against the higher-resolution ERA5 using the SyCLoPS tracker. JRA-3Q achieves substantially higher detection skill, with a hit rate of 90% and a false alarm rate of 6% during 1979-2024. Unlike ERA5, which exhibits markedly degraded detection skill during the pre-satellite era, JRA-3Q maintains stable performance over time. We analyze false alarms and missed TCs in the North Indian basin, TC vortex evolution following TC bogussing, and the spatial variance of column-integrated moist static energy, showing that JRA-3Q's improvements stem from both reduced model biases and a more effective and consistently applied TC bogus scheme. A decomposition of TC representation errors into contributions from tracking algorithm, reanalysis, and best-track uncertainty helps explain the sources of these biases.
item.dc:creator: Yushan Han, Paul A. Ullrich, Colin Zarzycki, Stella Bourdin

item.title: DaYu-TC: a global-regional nested AI system for tropical cyclone forecasting
item.description: arXiv:2611.15266v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Accurate tropical cyclone intensity forecasts are essential for disaster preparedness, yet persistent intensity underestimation limits the value of artificial intelligence (AI) weather models for predicting these destructive storms. Here we present DaYu-TC, a global-regional nested system that links the preservation of strong-wind and low-pressure signals with high-resolution regional prediction. Its global and regional models share an architecture and extreme-aware training objectives. The regional model combines evolving local states with global forecasts valid at each target time, connecting large-scale environmental information with finer-scale cyclone evolution. In an independent evaluation of 16 western North Pacific tropical cyclones in 2023, the global model retains competitive conventional forecast skill while reducing five-day maximum-wind root-mean-square error (RMSE) by 6-22% relative to other evaluated global AI models. Relative to the global model, regional nesting reduces maximum-wind RMSE by 22.0-33.1% and minimum-pressure RMSE by 28.6-39.8% across 12-120 h. The complete system outperforms concurrent operational high-resolution forecasts from the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts for minimum pressure at 12-120 h and maximum wind speed at 48-96 h, with respective RMSE reductions of 26% and 12% at 72 h. Without retraining, the same regional model enhances three other global AI models, reducing overall maximum-wind RMSE by 22.6-28.6%. Five-day forecasts take under one minute on a single GPU. These results establish a transferable multiscale approach to reducing cyclone intensity underestimation, extending advances in AI weather forecasting towards more accurate prediction of high-impact weather events.
item.dc:creator: Runzepu Hou, Feng Zhang, Xin Wu, Xujun Wei, Fenghua Ling, Kan Dai, Gaozhen Nie, Leiming Ma, Renhe Zhang

item.title: HybridCT: ML Accelerated Tomography for Climate Relevant 3D Cloud Observations
item.description: arXiv:2611.16255v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Low-level clouds are one of the largest sources of uncertainty in climate predictions, partly because we lack detailed three-dimensional (3D) measurements of their internal structure. Here, we present HybridCT, a cloud tomographic reconstruction scheme accelerated by machine learning (ML) that recovers 3D cloud extinction directly from passive multi-angle observations. An ML emulator maps radiances from multiple viewing angles to cloud optical thickness (COT), producing path-integrated projections, and a Simultaneous Algebraic Reconstruction Technique (SART) explicitly inverts these projections to retrieve 3D extinction. Training observations are generated from synthetic 3D cloud fields using radiative transfer simulations for nine viewing angles between $\pm$70$^{\circ}$. HybridCT reconstructs extinction with RMSE 13.3 km$^{-1}$ in 3.5 s, compared to 22.7 km$^{-1}$ in approx. 30 min for the state-of-the-art physics-based tomography framework AT3D, a speedup exceeding 500$\times$. HybridCT thus provides a scalable route toward large-scale observations of 3D cloud structure relevant to radiative-budget interpretation and evaluation of high-resolution cloud simulations.
item.dc:creator: Linda Forster, Nicholas J. LaHaye, Marcin J. Kurowski, Anna Jungbluth, Bernhard Mayer, Anthony B. Davis

item.title: Upscale energy transfer from mesoscale convective systems to African easterly waves
item.description: arXiv:2611.16941v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: African easterly waves (AEWs) drive the synoptic variability of West African monsoon rainfall via intricate two-way interactions with mesoscale convective systems (MCSs). The composite MCS-AEW system is a canonical example of multiscale interactions in the tropical atmosphere, with upscale feedbacks from deep convection driving the evolution of a larger-scale circulation. Here we support this perspective through application of techniques from turbulence theory, calculating for the first time patterns of interscale kinetic energy transfer, $\mathcal{D}_L$, across different spatial scales $L$ around MCSs and AEW lifecycle phases. We study AEW and MCS dynamics in two pan-tropical 40 day Met Office Unified Model simulations with $\sim$5km grid spacings, for which $\mathcal{D}_L$ is calculated with the LoSSETT software package. We find explicitly-simulated MCSs show a distinctive vertical dipole structure of $\mathcal{D}_L$ at scales below 1000km, with strong upscale energy transfer located in the upper troposphere within storm anvils. Regionally, upscale energy transfer occurs most strongly where organised convection is active. We find 200hPa upscale transfer consistently leads AEW troughs, and that growing continental AEWs in the explicit simulation are characterised by strengthened upscale transfer of energy from MCS to AEW scales. Case-study analysis shows this transfer can contribute to the eddy kinetic energy growth of strengthening AEW troughs. These signals are weak in a simulation with parameterised convection: here, zonal mean energetics show enhanced barotropic conversion, caused by a stronger African Easterly Jet, provides a stronger AEW population. Our analysis of upscale energy transfers complements previous analysis of AEW potential vorticity dynamics, providing a route towards building new theoretical understanding of tropical dynamics from km-scale models.
item.dc:creator: Ben Maybee, Elliot McKinnon-Gray, Dan Shipley, John Methven

item.title: Towards Distributed Quantum Computing: Quantum Gate Teleportation via Satellite-Distributed Entanglement under Atmospheric Depolarization
item.description: arXiv:2611.14623v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We investigate quantum gate teleportation as a primitive for satellite-enabled distributed quantum computing. In the considered architecture, a satellite distributes entangled photon pairs to two optical ground stations, which transfer the shared quantum resource to remote quantum processing units. This entanglement is then used to implement a nonlocal controlled-NOT gate between two circuit qubits located in different processors. We formulate the minimal four-qubit protocol, consisting of two network qubits that provide the entangled resource and two circuit qubits on which the distributed gate is performed. Atmospheric propagation effects in the gravitational field are modeled through an effective two-qubit depolarizing channel whose parameters depend on atmospheric and optical quantities, including the Fried parameter and receiver aperture. The performance of the protocol is quantified by the fidelity between the ideal CNOT output state and the state produced by noisy quantum gate teleportation. Our results show that the fidelity is governed by the quality of the distributed entanglement and depends jointly on atmospheric coherence, aperture size, and effective depolarization strength. These findings connect physical-layer modeling of satellite optical channels with gate-level performance in distributed quantum computing.
item.dc:creator: Artur Czerwinski, Jakub J. Borkowski, Maciej Wi\'sniewski, Saeed Haddadi

item.title: Fragility of Aeolian Ripples
item.description: arXiv:2611.14739v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Sand surfaces exposed to the wind are covered by aeolian sand waves of diverse wavelengths, from centimetres for small ripples to decameters for dunes. Sand dunes can be said to be antifragile, since their growth is not prohibited by storms, whereas ripples and megaripples are fragile since they get flattened. The fluid-entrainment hypothesis attributes their fragility to a common cause: the spontaneous aerodynamic entrainment of grains. Here, we challenge this conventional view by revealing its major shortcomings and inconsistencies. An alternative framework, routed in the granular bed rheology, posits that impact ripples are erased when the two-phase flow of ballistically hopping grains on a solid sand surface gives way to a three-phase flow, featuring an intermediate, collision-dominated, fluid-like transport layer. Notably, both martian wind-drag ripples and terrestrial aerodynamic ripples, which emerge via a hydrodynamic instability, are insensitive to such "surface-melting". Their destruction is predicated on the transition from aerodynamically smooth to rough conditions, instead. Our theoretical arguments are well supported by a stability diagram in terms of Shields number and grain diameter, assembled from a carefully reassessed large body of literature, and backed up by dedicated control measurements.
item.dc:creator: Constantin Rein, Katharina Tholen, Lior Saban, Itzhak Katra, Hezi Yizhaq, Klaus Kroy

item.title: Turbulent velocity statistics in convective boundary layers
item.description: arXiv:2611.14805v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Large-eddy simulations (LES) of the convective atmospheric boundary layer (CBL) are used to investigate velocity variance statistics in turbulent sheared convection. The thirteen simulations span conditions from weak convection with longitudinal rolls to free penetrative convection with no mean wind. In the presence of thermal rolls, the near-surface streamwise variance profile exhibits an approximately logarithmic decay with a slope proportional to the friction velocity, $u_*$, and an added constant proportional to the convective velocity, $w_\star$. After the structural transition to convective cells, both the streamwise and spanwise variances follow the empirical stability and height dependencies of Wilson (\textit{Boundary-Layer Meteorol.}, 2008, vol. 129, pp. 353--369). The near-surface vertical (wall-normal) velocity variance is well described by Monin--Obukhov similarity with improved agreement using local-in-height scaling. Within the mixed layer, the peak vertical variance initially decreases relative to $w_\star$ as shear diminishes, before increasing and shifting downward as the flow approaches free convection. In contrast, the total turbulent energy decreases relative to $w_\star$ across the parameter space. The spanwise velocity variance represents the dominant turbulent component under weak convection and exceeds the streamwise variance throughout most of the convective regime. These statistical trends are attributed to the role of pressure, evaluated through variance budget contributions. Large-scale buoyancy production in the mixed layer is transported downward by pressure and redistributed preferentially to the spanwise component, coinciding with the presence of longitudinal roll motions. The weakening of this pressure-transport pathway for convective cells coincides with greater retention of vertical variance within the mixed layer.
item.dc:creator: Aditya Chaudhary, Marcelo Chamecki, Michael Heisel

item.title: Data-driven Reconstruction of the Phase Dynamics for the El Ni\~{n}o-Southern Oscillation Reveals Seasonality and Statistical Synchronization with the Annual Cycle
item.description: arXiv:2611.14868v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: In this study, we treat the El Ni\~{n}o-Southern Oscillation (ENSO) as a rhythmic system periodically forced by the annual cycle. We examine ENSO event seasonality and synchronization between the annual and ENSO cycles. We compute phase time series for both cycles from sea surface temperature data using a data-driven Koopman operator approach. We then use Bayesian inference to reconstruct phase equations describing how the phases of the two oscillators evolve. The reconstructed two-variable phase equations show that the annual cycle modulates the instantaneous frequency of the fundamental ENSO mode. Stochastic simulations of these equations incorporating the estimated stationary noise indicate that El Ni\~{n}o and La Ni\~{n}a events tend to last longer when they start in boreal summer and that the variability of their durations is greater when they start in boreal spring. Furthermore, the averaged form of the phase equations indicates statistical $3:1$ phase locking between the annual and ENSO cycles, whereas no statistical phase locking is found for the other $m:n$ ratios.
item.dc:creator: Takahiro Arai, Yoji Kawamura

item.title: Tendex Lines and Short-Time Deformation: The Geometry of Lunar Tides
item.description: arXiv:2611.16083v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Tendex lines and the stretchlines and squeezelines of Lagrangian coherent structure theory share a geometric construction: they integrate eigenvector fields of symmetric tensors. We connect their dynamical interpretations through the short-time deformation of particles released with zero initial velocity relative to a freely falling reference in an autonomous gravitational field. The leading departure of the Cauchy--Green tensor from the identity is quadratic in time and equals the tidal tensor multiplied by the squared observation time. The tidal tensorlines therefore give the limiting principal stretching and squeezing directions. For the planar lunar field, these tensorlines are radial lines and concentric circles centered on the Moon. The same tidal tensor defines a Lorentzian metric whose null directions have no quadratic change in line-element length. Its null geodesics are logarithmic spirals, describing the short-time limit of finite-time unit-stretch geometry. Near Earth, the principal tensorlines clarify the two outward tidal tendencies, while the null directions distinguish vanishing leading extension from vanishing relative acceleration.
item.dc:creator: F. J. Beron-Vera

item.title: Access to the quasi-geostrophic model from within the BK19 compressible flow solver
item.description: arXiv:2611.16601v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We extend BK19 the semi-implicit finite-volume solver, to provide access to the quasi-geostrophic (QG) regime within the same compressible framework that already admits soundproof and hydrostatic limits. In order to achieve this goal, we incorporate the asymptotic framework from the continuous theory into the numerical scheme. Adopting the usual asymptotic setting for the quasi-geostrophic regime and using it directly in the numerical model, we perform a scale analysis of the compressible Euler equations in the synoptic length and time scales in the limit of small Rossby number. In this limit, the discrete implicit step recovers geostrophic balance, together with the pseudo-incompressible divergence constraint. We construct a staggered-grid curl operator consistent with the discrete derivatives and use it to define the vorticity in the numerical framework. An asymptotic analysis of the fully discrete scheme then yields a Poisson-type equation for the leading-order Exner-pressure perturbation that coincides with the QG pressure Poisson equation in the continuous theory. As a result of this analysis, we introduce two additional blending switches that (i) convert the elliptic pressure problem from the full Helmholtz to its QG Poisson-type equation and (ii) control whether the horizontal momenta are updated prognostically or diagnosed from geostrophic balance. In combination with the existing soundproof and hydrostatic switches, the resulting algorithm can be operated in fully compressible, pseudo-incompressible, hydrostatic, and QG modes without changing the underlying discretization. The functionality of the numerical scheme in the QG regime is then tested by two idealized vortex test cases to show how stable the vortices remain in the QG run and that, as the Rossby number is reduced, the full compressible scheme converges to slow, balanced QG dynamics.
item.dc:creator: Amir Maghoul, Rupert Klein

item.title: Scaling Storm-Resolving Atmospheric AI Simulation to the Entire Planet
item.description: arXiv:2606.31248v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Kilometer-scale convection shapes precipitation extremes, tropical organization, and cloud feedbacks, but most global atmospheric models approximate these processes at 25-100 km resolution. Global storm-resolving physics models resolve convective systems explicitly, but at a cost (roughly one MWh per simulated day on exascale supercomputers) that limits long-duration simulation. We introduce STRATA (Storm-resolving Tile-based autoRegressive Atmosphere Transformer Architecture), the first autoregressive AI emulator for global storm-resolving atmospheric dynamics. STRATA is trained on the highest-resolution atmospheric dataset yet used for global AI emulation: 17 days of SCREAM physics-model output at 4.9-km resolution (~25 million grid cells) sampled every 10 minutes. Our central premise is that on 10-minute timescales atmospheric dynamics are predominantly local, so training on small spatial tiles trades scarce global temporal samples for abundant local spatial samples and enables global rollout via overlapping-tile blending. STRATA combines 3D patch embedding and local 3D neighborhood attention, a novel Stereographic Rotary Position Embedding (StereoRoPE) for grid-invariant encoding, and a pixel-space de-aliasing decoder that suppresses patch-scale rollout artifacts. An iso-FLOP scaling study reveals that km-scale emulation requires ~10x more FLOPs per grid point than coarse-resolution AI weather models, consistent with the higher information density of convective-scale dynamics. Trained on only 17 days of data, STRATA produces stable 24-hour global rollouts with realistic km-scale dynamics across diverse regimes, though large-scale biases develop with lead time. It achieves 48 simulated days per megawatt-hour (more than 50 times better energy efficiency than the SCREAM physics model) and 741 simulated days per wall-clock day at 512 H100 GPUs.
item.dc:creator: Zeyuan Hu, Akshay Subramaniam, Noel Keen, Tao Ge, Jaideep Pathak, Mohammad Shoaib Abbas, Suman Ravuri, Karthik Kashinath, Naser Mahfouz, Peter Caldwell, Mike Pritchard, Noah Brenowitz

item.title: Coupled multiscale paleoclimate reconstruction with four-dimensional variational data assimilation
item.description: arXiv:2608.19469v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Paleoclimate archives extend climate knowledge beyond the instrumental era, registering different seasons, variables, time averages, and memory lengths. A longstanding problem is to integrate these heterogeneous sources of information within a unified methodology. Here we present a new data-assimilation framework, Last Millennium Reanalysis 4D-Var (LMR4D-Var), which reconstructs climate trajectories from these heterogeneous datasets while balancing errors in the model, observations, and initial conditions. We compare results using LMR4D-Var to assimilate proxies from PAGES2k, Temp12k, and borehole temperature profiles without treating them as instantaneous equivalents. Instrumental validation demonstrates that LMR4D-Var achieves the highest skill in reconstructing global mean temperature among existing reconstructions. Borehole assimilation preserves skill against withheld annually resolved records, increases agreement between reconstructed 300--2000-m ocean heat content (OHC) and independent estimates, and yields a cooler reconstructed Little Ice Age ocean. Modern 130-year OHC trends in the 0--300-m and 300--2000-m layers exceed their respective reconstructed pre-1870 Common Era trend distributions. Results for Temp12k demonstrate assimilation of decadal-to-millennial records and the potential for Holocene and deeper-time applications with suitable emulators.
item.dc:creator: Zilu Meng, Gregory J. Hakim, Julien Emile-Geay, Tanaya Gondhalekar, Eric J. Steig

item.title: Predicting tipping points: The many shades of non-equilibrium and catch-22s of early-warning
item.description: arXiv:2609.10378v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The potential of crossing climate tipping points has reached the attention of many researchers and the general public. On the one hand, the basis for this concern is strengthening, with simulations showing abrupt transitions that may occur even for moderate greenhouse gas emission scenarios. On the other hand, our understanding of what constitutes such transitions mathematically is becoming more nuanced. This leads to challenges for the fidelity of early-warning signals (EWS), which accompany bifurcations in systems that closely track a slowly changing steady state. Different kinds of out-of-equilibrium dynamics in a rapidly changing climate, as well as chaos, blur the notion of a critical tipping threshold and imply limits in predictability. Using EWS to detect loss of local stability from data requires careful evaluation in the high-dimensional system, and may have limited predictive power in a highly multistable climate, where there is more than a single, well-known alternative state. This calls for new methods using non-equilibrium statistical mechanics and dynamical systems to efficiently probe the global stability properties of climate models and observations.
item.dc:creator: Johannes Lohmann

item.title: Direct Multispectral Satellite Nowcasting of Gridded Surface Solar Radiation
item.description: arXiv:2611.12999v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Surface shortwave radiation (SWR) can change within minutes as clouds evolve, but operational forecasts often trade spatial detail and update frequency for forecast range. Here, we present a numerical-weather-prediction-independent, observation-to-forecast framework that converts sequences of Himawari-9 Level-1 multispectral imagery and solar geometry directly into 24 gridded SWR fields at 10-min intervals for the next 4 h. A controlled six-model experiment in eastern China separates the effects of satellite information from those of temporal self-attention. In the 0-1 h window, the full-multispectral attention model achieves a mean absolute error of 37.9 W/m2 and a root mean square error of 63.7 W/m2, reductions of 21.0% and 19.5% relative to a historical-SWR baseline. Improvements extend across nine subregions and include weaker spatial bias and better structural consistency. Temporal attention does not improve forecasts from historical SWR alone, but becomes effective when supplied with multispectral cloud and thermodynamic signals. Direct multispectral observations therefore provide the precursor information required for high-frequency, spatially resolved SWR nowcasting.
item.dc:creator: Tianyu Xie, Zhaoliang Zeng, Zhehao Liang, Ke Gui, Xutao Zhang, Yaqiang Wang, Dabo Guan, Huizheng Che

item.title: PQG-DL-Ekman: a triple-deck boundary layer theory for large-scale atmospheric flow with moist process closures
item.description: arXiv:2504.20191v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Reduced mathematical models for atmospheric dynamics at various scales have a long and rich history. However, versions of such models that explicitly incorporate moisture and phase changes have been developed only fairly recently. This work merges one of said modeling innovations, namely Smith and Stechmann's \emph{precipitating quasigeostrophic} (PQG) model family, with a triple-deck boundary layer theory due to Klein et al.~that extends the classical QG-Ekman theory by an intermediate \emph{diabatic layer} (DL). A detailed analysis of the Clausius-Clapeyron relation and Kessler-type bulk microphysics closures is included in the systematic derivation of the resulting PQG-DL-Ekman theory. Furthermore, to illustrate some of the model's properties, explicit axisymmetric solutions of the precipitating diabatic layer equations are derived and combined with numerical sample solutions for the bulk flow.
item.dc:creator: Daniel B\"aumer, Rupert Klein

item.title: Sea Surface Roughness Dependence on Ocean Wave Parameters through Large Eddy Simulation with Local Subfilter Wave Drag
item.description: arXiv:2606.15446v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Characterizing the Marine Atmospheric Boundary Layer (MABL) requires understanding the coupling between ocean waves and the turbulent atmospheric boundary layer above them. This coupling controls momentum exchange between the atmosphere and the ocean; it is of practical importance in the global climate, flow of ocean currents, ocean engineering, and offshore wind energy. Computational study of the MABL is complex because it must resolve the coupled physics of waves and turbulence over a wide range of spatial and temporal scales. This study expands on approaches for representing dynamic, local waves in Large Eddy Simulations (LES) of the MABL by developing a subfilter wave drag model to be local and scale-invariant. It explores the effects of different wave parameters (significant wave height and peak frequency of the wave energy spectrum) on the resulting momentum flux beyond monotonic relationships between surface stress through friction velocity $u_\ast$ and wind velocity above the surface $U_{10}$. Results are compared to field data and in a discussion on how representation of the MABL and associated momentum flux need to account for both wind and wave effects.
item.dc:creator: Hannah Hata Williams, Aditya K. Aiyer, Luc Deike, Michael E. Mueller
